report:
Conclusion: the blanket claim is **false/unsupported**. The concern began as a *theoretical* hypothesis: a *Lancet Respiratory Medicine* correspondence suggested ibuprofen might upregulate ACE2, the receptor SARS‑CoV‑2 uses, potentially increasing susceptibility or severity (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanres/article/PIIS2213-2600(20)30158-2/fulltext). That was not clinical outcome evidence.

Later clinical evidence did not confirm the fear. A systematic review/meta-analysis concluded the “theoretical risks of NSAIDs or ibuprofen in SARS‑CoV‑2 infection are not confirmed by observational data” (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34339037/). Fact-checking of the early claims likewise found no evidence that ibuprofen/NSAIDs make COVID‑19 more severe (https://www.factcheck.org/2020/03/no-evidence-to-back-covid-19-ibuprofen-concerns/). UK guidance shifted to say ibuprofen can be used for COVID‑19 symptoms, though reasons for the change were initially unclear (https://www.bmj.com/content/369/bmj.m1555).

Important nuance: “not shown to worsen COVID‑19” does not mean risk-free. Ibuprofen still has known gastrointestinal, kidney, blood-pressure, pregnancy, and drug-interaction risks; observational studies can suffer confounding because sicker people may take different medicines. For most adults, short-term use at the lowest effective dose is reasonable when appropriate, but people with kidney disease, ulcers/bleeding risk, cardiovascular disease, pregnancy, or those on interacting medicines should ask a clinician; paracetamol/acetaminophen is often preferred first for fever when suitable.
